<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:CT}
The lift $\widetilde j:\mathbb H^2\to\mathbb H^3$ extends continuously to a map
\[
\widehat j:\mathbb H^2\cup S^1\longrightarrow\mathbb H^3\cup S^2 .
\]
The boundary map $\partial\iota:=\widehat j|_{S^1}:S^1\to S^2$ is $\rho$--equivariant and surjective; in particular it is a Peano curve.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:bounded}
Let $u,v:\mathbb H^2\to\mathbb H^3$ be continuous maps with
\[
\sup_{z\in\mathbb H^2}d_{\mathbb H^3}(u(z),v(z))<\infty.
\]
Suppose that $v$ extends continuously to
\(\widehat v:\mathbb H^2\cup S^1\to \mathbb H^3\cup S^2\) with $\widehat v(S^1)\subset S^2$.  Then $u$ has a unique continuous extension $\widehat u:\mathbb H^2\cup S^1\to \mathbb H^3\cup S^2$, and
\(\widehat u|_{S^1}=\widehat v|_{S^1}\).
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $C=\sup_z d(u(z),v(z))$ and define $\widehat u=u$ on $\mathbb H^2$ and $\widehat u=\widehat v$ on $S^1$.  Both compactifications are metrizable, so it suffices to check sequential continuity at points $\xi\in S^1$.  Let $z_n\to\xi$ in $\mathbb H^2\cup S^1$.  For the terms $z_n\in S^1$ we have $\widehat u(z_n)=\widehat v(z_n)\to\widehat v(\xi)$.  For the terms $z_n\in\mathbb H^2$ we have $v(z_n)\to\widehat v(\xi)\in S^2$ and $d(u(z_n),v(z_n))\le C$.  In $\mathbb H^3$, if $x_n\to\zeta\in S^2$ and $d(x_n,y_n)\le C$, then the Gromov products satisfy $(x_n\cdot y_n)_o\ge d(o,x_n)-C\to\infty$, so $y_n\to\zeta$.  Hence $u(z_n)\to\widehat v(\xi)$.  Uniqueness holds because $\mathbb H^2$ is dense in $\mathbb H^2\cup S^1$ and the target is Hausdorff.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:equivariantbounded}
Let a group $G$ act on a topological space $Y$ and by isometries on a metric space $Z$, and suppose there is a compact set $K\subset Y$ with $G\cdot K=Y$.  If $a,b:Y\to Z$ are continuous and $G$--equivariant, then
\(\sup_{y\in Y}d_Z(a(y),b(y))<\infty\).
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The function $y\mapsto d(a(y),b(y))$ is continuous, hence bounded on $K$, and it is $G$--invariant because $d(a(\gamma y),b(\gamma y))=d(\gamma a(y),\gamma b(y))=d(a(y),b(y))$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:anyrepresentative}
Let $X$ be a marked hyperbolic structure on $S$ and let $u:\mathbb H^2\to\mathbb H^3$ be a continuous $\rho$--equivariant map.  Then $u$ extends continuously to $\mathbb H^2\cup S^1$, and its boundary map is $\partial\iota$.  In particular this holds for the $\rho$--equivariant lift of any continuous map $a:S\to M_f$ homotopic to $j$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:equivariantbounded} to $u$ and $\widetilde j$, with $K$ a closed fundamental polygon for $\rho_X(G)$; then apply Lemma~\ref{lem:bounded} with $v=\widetilde j$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:CT}.  If $H:S\times[0,1]\to M_f$ is a homotopy from $j$ to $a$, lifting $H$ with initial map $\widetilde j$ gives a lift $\widetilde a$ of $a$; for each $\gamma\in G$ the maps $\widetilde H_s\circ\rho_X(\gamma)$ and $\rho(\gamma)\circ\widetilde H_s$ are lifts of $H_s$ agreeing at $s=0$, hence for all $s$, so $\widetilde a$ is $\rho$--equivariant.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:otherlifts}
Every other lift of $a$ has the form $\delta\circ\widetilde a$ with $\delta\in\Gamma$; it is equivariant for $\gamma\mapsto\delta\rho(\gamma)\delta^{-1}$, and its boundary map is $\delta\circ\partial\iota$.  Such a map has the same image $S^2$ as $\partial\iota$.  If $\delta\in G$, it induces the same equivalence relation on $S^1$ as $\partial\iota$: indeed $\delta\circ\partial\iota=\partial\iota\circ\rho_X(\delta)$, so postcomposition by $\delta$ only relabels the image points.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:markings}
Let $\psi:S\to S$ be a homeomorphism.  Then $j\circ\psi$ is freely homotopic to $j$ if and only if $\psi$ is isotopic to $f^n$ for some $n\in\mathbb Z$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The homotopy $H_s(x)=[x,s]$, $s\in[0,1]$, goes from $j$ to $j\circ f$; iterating, $j\circ f^n\simeq j$ for all $n$.  Conversely, $M_f$ is aspherical, so free homotopy classes of maps $S\to M_f$ correspond to $\Gamma$--conjugacy classes of homomorphisms $G\to\Gamma$.  If $j\circ\psi\simeq j$, then $\iota\circ\psi_*=c_\delta\circ\iota$ for some $\delta\in\Gamma$, where $\psi_*$ is defined up to an inner automorphism of $G$.  Writing $\delta=\gamma t^n$ with $\gamma\in G$, the outer class of $\psi_*$ equals that of $f_*^n$.  By the Dehn--Nielsen--Baer theorem and the fact that homotopic homeomorphisms of a closed surface are isotopic \cite{FM}, $\psi$ is isotopic to $f^n$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:ESHartman}
For every $X\in\mathcal T$ there is a unique harmonic map $h_X:(S,\sigma_X)\to M_f$ freely homotopic to $j$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Existence follows from the Eells--Sampson theorem, since $S$ and $M_f$ are compact and $M_f$ has sectional curvature $-1$.  By Hartman's theorem, two homotopic harmonic maps into a compact manifold of negative sectional curvature coincide unless their image is contained in a closed geodesic or is a point.  A map with image in a closed geodesic induces a homomorphism with cyclic image, whereas maps homotopic to $j$ induce a homomorphism with image conjugate to the nonabelian group $G$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:harmonicCT}
For every $X\in\mathcal T$, the $\rho$--equivariant lift
\(\widetilde h_X:\mathbb H^2\to\mathbb H^3\)
of $h_X$ extends continuously to
\(\widehat h_X:\mathbb H^2\cup S^1\to\mathbb H^3\cup S^2\), and
\(\widehat h_X|_{S^1}=\partial\iota\).
In particular
\(\widehat h_X(S^1)=S^2\).
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:anyrepresentative} to $a=h_X$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:Xindependent}
Let $X,Y\in\mathcal T$.  Under the identifications $\partial\mathbb H^2_X\cong\partial G\cong\partial\mathbb H^2_Y$ of Section~1, the boundary maps of $\widetilde h_X$ and $\widetilde h_Y$ coincide.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:leastarea}
There is a smooth embedded surface $\Sigma_{\min}\subset M_f$, isotopic to the fiber $j(S)$, with $\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma_{\min})=A_0$.  In particular $\Sigma_{\min}$ is a stable minimal surface.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Since $j_*$ is injective, the least-area existence theorem for incompressible maps gives a smooth least-area immersion in this homotopy class; see Schoen--Yau \cite{SY}, Sacks--Uhlenbeck \cite{SU}, and the formulation in Hass--Scott \cite{HS}.  Freedman--Hass--Scott \cite{FHS} show that, because the class contains the two-sided embedding $j$, a least-area immersion is either an embedding or a double cover of an embedded one-sided surface $P$.  The manifold $M_f$ is orientable because $S$ is orientable and $f$ is orientation preserving.  Hence a one-sided surface $P$ has a nontrivial orientation double cover.  The second case cannot occur.  Indeed, the image of $\pi_1(P)$ in $\Gamma$ would contain $G$ with index two.  Since $G\triangleleft\Gamma$, its image in $\Gamma/G\cong\mathbb Z$ would therefore be finite, hence trivial; thus $\pi_1(P)$ would be contained in $G$, contradicting $[\pi_1(P):G]=2$.  Hence the least-area immersion is an embedding.  It is incompressible and homotopic to the fiber; since $M_f$ is Haken, Waldhausen's theorem \cite{Wald} implies that it is isotopic to the fiber.  A global area minimizer in its homotopy class is minimal, and its second variation is nonnegative, so it is stable.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:minimalPeano}
The $\rho$--equivariant lift $F:\mathbb H^2\to\mathbb H^3$ of $u_0$, with $\mathbb H^2$ the universal cover of $X_{\min}$, has the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $F$ is a conformal harmonic embedding, and $F(\mathbb H^2)$ is a connected component of the preimage of $\Sigma_{\min}$ in $\mathbb H^3$;
\item $F(\mathbb H^2)$ is complete in the induced metric and properly embedded in $\mathbb H^3$;
\item $F$ extends continuously to
\(\widehat F:\mathbb H^2\cup S^1\to\mathbb H^3\cup S^2\);
\item $\widehat F|_{S^1}=\partial\iota$; in particular $\widehat F(S^1)=S^2$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $\widetilde\Sigma$ be the component of the preimage of $\Sigma_{\min}$ containing $F(\mathbb H^2)$.  The covering $\widetilde\Sigma\to\Sigma_{\min}$ corresponds to the kernel of $\pi_1(\Sigma_{\min})\to\pi_1(M_f)$, which is trivial; so $\widetilde\Sigma$ is simply connected, and $F:\mathbb H^2\to\widetilde\Sigma$ is a lift of the diffeomorphism $u_0$ between universal covers, hence a diffeomorphism.  Since $u_0$ is conformal and minimal, $F$ is conformal and harmonic.  As $F$ is a diffeomorphism onto the embedded component $\widetilde\Sigma$, it is an embedding.  The preimage of the closed set $\Sigma_{\min}$ is a closed embedded surface in $\mathbb H^3$, and its components are closed; so $\widetilde\Sigma$ is properly embedded.  It is complete in its induced metric because it covers the compact surface $\Sigma_{\min}$.  Items (iii) and (iv) follow from Proposition~\ref{prop:anyrepresentative} and Theorem~\ref{thm:CT}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:Hopfzero}
With $X_{\min}$ as above, $h_{X_{\min}}=u_0$.  Consequently
\(\Phi_{X_{\min}}=0\).
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The map $u_0:(S,X_{\min})\to M_f$ is conformal and minimal, hence harmonic, and it is homotopic to $j$.  Theorem~\ref{thm:ESHartman} gives $u_0=h_{X_{\min}}$, and $\operatorname{Hopf}(u_0)=0$ because $u_0$ is conformal.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:area-curvature}
If $\Sigma$ is stable, then
\[
2\pi(g-1)< \operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)<4\pi(g-1),
\qquad
0<\int_{\Sigma}|A|^2\,dA=8\pi(g-1)-2\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)<4\pi(g-1),
\]
and
\[
-2<\frac{1}{\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)}\int_{\Sigma}K_{\Sigma}\,dA<-1 .
\]
The upper bound $\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)<4\pi(g-1)$ holds without the stability assumption.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Integrating the Gauss equation and using Gauss--Bonnet,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:GB}
\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)+\frac12\int_{\Sigma}|A|^2\,dA=4\pi(g-1).
\end{equation}
Thus $\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)\leq4\pi(g-1)$, with equality exactly when $A\equiv0$.  In that case a lift of $\Sigma$ to $\mathbb H^3$ is a totally geodesic plane invariant under a conjugate of $G$, and the limit set of $G$ would be a round circle.  The limit set of $G$ is $S^2$ (Section~1), so the upper bound is strict.

The Jacobi operator of $\Sigma$ is $L=\Delta+|A|^2+\operatorname{Ric}(N,N)=\Delta+|A|^2-2$.  Stability, applied to the constant test function $1$, gives $\int_\Sigma(|A|^2-2)\,dA\le0$.  Together with \eqref{eq:GB} this gives $\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)\geq2\pi(g-1)$.  If equality holds, the quadratic form $Q(\varphi)=\int_\Sigma(|\nabla\varphi|^2-(|A|^2-2)\varphi^2)\,dA$, which is nonnegative, vanishes at $\varphi=1$; so $1$ lies in the kernel of $L$, and $|A|^2\equiv2$, that is, $k\equiv1$.  A surface in a hyperbolic $3$--manifold whose principal curvatures are constant and distinct is flat: in a principal frame $e_1,e_2$, the Codazzi equations give $(k_1-k_2)\,\omega_{12}(e_i)=0$ for $i=1,2$, so $\omega_{12}=0$.  The Cartan structure equation $d\omega_{12}=-K_\Sigma\,\omega_1\wedge\omega_2$ then gives $K_\Sigma=0$.  This contradicts $K_\Sigma=-2$.  Hence the lower bound is strict.  The remaining statements follow from \eqref{eq:GB} and $\int_\Sigma K_\Sigma\,dA=-4\pi(g-1)$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:maxcurv}
Let $u:S\to M_f$ be a smooth immersion homotopic to $j$.  Then at some point of $S$ some principal curvature of $u$ has absolute value at least $1$.  In particular every closed minimal surface in $M_f$ homotopic to the fiber satisfies
\[
\max_\Sigma k\geq1,\qquad \max_\Sigma|A|^2\geq2,\qquad \min_\Sigma K_\Sigma\leq-2 .
\]
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Suppose that all principal curvatures of $u$ have absolute value at most $k_0<1$; by compactness this is the negation of the conclusion.  Let $\widetilde u:\mathbb H^2\to\mathbb H^3$ be the $\rho$--equivariant lift, with the induced complete metric $g_u$ and unit normal $N$, and let $E:\mathbb H^2\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb H^3$, $E(x,s)=\exp_{\widetilde u(x)}(sN(x))$.  Jacobi fields in curvature $-1$ give
\[
E^*g_{\mathbb H^3}=ds^2+g_u\big((\cosh s\,I-\sinh s\,W)\cdot,(\cosh s\,I-\sinh s\,W)\cdot\big),
\]
where $W$ is the shape operator.  The eigenvalues of $\cosh s\,I-\sinh s\,W$ are $\cosh s-k_i\sinh s=\sqrt{1-k_i^2}\,\cosh(s-\operatorname{artanh}k_i)\geq\sqrt{1-k_0^2}$.  Hence
\[
E^*g_{\mathbb H^3}\geq ds^2+(1-k_0^2)\,g_u .
\]
The right side is a complete metric, so $E^*g_{\mathbb H^3}$ is complete.  Since $E^*g_{\mathbb H^3}$ is positive definite, $dE$ is nonsingular everywhere; thus $E$ is a local diffeomorphism, and with the pullback metric it is a local isometry.  By the standard covering theorem for complete local isometries, $E$ is a covering map onto the connected manifold $\mathbb H^3$; since $\mathbb H^3$ is simply connected, $E$ is a diffeomorphism.  Let $P=\mathrm{pr}_1\circ E^{-1}:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^2$.  By the inequality above, $P$ multiplies lengths of curves by at most $(1-k_0^2)^{-1/2}$, and $P\circ\widetilde u=\mathrm{id}$.  Therefore
\[
d_{g_u}(x,y)\leq(1-k_0^2)^{-1/2}\,d_{\mathbb H^3}(\widetilde u(x),\widetilde u(y)),
\]
and $d_{\mathbb H^3}(\widetilde u(x),\widetilde u(y))\le d_{g_u}(x,y)$.  Since $g_u$ is $G$--invariant and $S$ is compact, $g_u$ is bi-Lipschitz to $\sigma_X$ for any $X$.  So $\widetilde u$ is a quasi-isometric embedding, and its boundary extension is injective.  By Proposition~\ref{prop:anyrepresentative} this extension is $\partial\iota$, which is not injective.  For a minimal surface the principal curvatures are $\pm k$, and the remaining inequalities follow from the Gauss equation.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:A2range}
For a stable minimal surface $\Sigma$ isotopic to the fiber,
\[
\min_\Sigma|A|^2<2\leq\max_\Sigma|A|^2 .
\]
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
By Proposition~\ref{prop:area-curvature}, the mean value of $|A|^2$ is $(8\pi(g-1)-2\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma))/\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)$, which is less than $2$ because $\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)>2\pi(g-1)$.  The upper inequality is Proposition~\ref{prop:maxcurv}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:strict-contraction}
Let $F:\mathbb H^2\to\mathbb H^3$ be the map of Theorem~\ref{thm:minimalPeano}, and let $\sigma$ be the hyperbolic metric on $\mathbb H^2$, the universal cover of $X_{\min}$.  Then $F^*g_{\mathbb H^3}<\sigma$ at every point, and there is $c\in(0,1)$ with $F^*g_{\mathbb H^3}\leq c^2\sigma$.  In particular
\[
d_{\mathbb H^3}(F(x),F(y))\leq c\,d_{\sigma}(x,y)
\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb H^2).
\]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Write $F^*g_{\mathbb H^3}=e^{2w}\sigma$, where $w$ is $G$--invariant and descends to $S$.  The curvature of $e^{2w}\sigma$ is $K=e^{-2w}(-1-\Delta_\sigma w)$, and $K=-1-\tfrac12|A|^2\le-1$; hence
\[
\Delta_\sigma w\ \geq\ e^{2w}-1 .
\]
At a maximum point of $w$ on the compact surface $S$ we have $\Delta_\sigma w\le0$, so $w\le0$ everywhere (this is the Ahlfors--Schwarz lemma \cite{Ahlfors} in the present setting).  Write $e^{2w}-1=\beta w$ with $\beta=(e^{2w}-1)/w\geq0$ (and $\beta=2$ where $w=0$).  Then $\Delta_\sigma w-\beta w\geq0$ and $w\le0$; by the strong maximum principle either $w\equiv0$ or $w<0$ everywhere (compare \cite{Minda}).  If $w\equiv0$, then $K\equiv-1$ and $A\equiv0$, which is excluded by Proposition~\ref{prop:area-curvature}.  Hence $w<0$, and $c=e^{\max_S w}<1$.  Integrating along curves gives the distance estimate.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:exponential-distortion}
There are constants $C\ge1$ and $0<a\le b$ such that
\[
C^{-1}e^{ar}-C\ \leq\ \operatorname{Dist}(r)\ \leq\ Ce^{br}\qquad(r\geq1).
\]
In particular $\widetilde\Sigma$ is not quasi-isometrically embedded in $\mathbb H^3$ and is not quasiconvex.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The group $G$ acts properly and cocompactly by isometries on $\widetilde\Sigma$ with its intrinsic metric, and $\Gamma$ acts properly and cocompactly on $\mathbb H^3$.  Fix $x_0\in\widetilde\Sigma$ and finite generating sets $\mathcal S_G$ of $G$ and $\mathcal S_G\cup\{t\}$ of $\Gamma$.  By the Milnor--\v{S}varc lemma, $\gamma\mapsto\gamma x_0$ is a quasi-isometry from $(G,|\cdot|_G)$ to $\widetilde\Sigma$ and from $(\Gamma,|\cdot|_\Gamma)$ to $\mathbb H^3$; the points of $\widetilde\Sigma$ are within bounded intrinsic distance of $Gx_0$.  It therefore suffices to prove the corresponding estimates for $\max\{|\gamma|_G:\gamma\in G,\ |\gamma|_\Gamma\le n\}$.

Let $\alpha=c_t|_G$.  For the lower bound, take $\gamma\in G\setminus\{1\}$.  The element $t^n\gamma t^{-n}=\alpha^n(\gamma)$ has $|\alpha^n(\gamma)|_\Gamma\leq2n+|\gamma|_\Gamma$.  The conjugacy class of $\alpha^n(\gamma)$ is the class of $f^{\pm n}(\gamma)$, because $\alpha$ represents the outer automorphism class of $f_*^{\pm1}$.  On the fixed compact hyperbolic surface $(S,\sigma_X)$, conjugacy length in $G$ is comparable with the length of the corresponding closed geodesic, and the latter grows exponentially like $\lambda^n$ for every nontrivial conjugacy class under a pseudo-Anosov map \cite{FLP}.  Since ordinary word length dominates conjugacy length, this gives the required exponential lower bound.  For the upper bound, a word of length $n$ in $\mathcal S_G\cup\{t^{\pm1}\}$ representing an element of $G$ has total $t$--exponent zero, so it can be rewritten as a product of at most $n$ elements $t^{e}st^{-e}=\alpha^{e}(s)$ with $s\in\mathcal S_G$ and $|e|\le n$.  Put $D=\max\bigl(\{2\}\cup\{|\alpha^{\pm1}(s)|_G:s\in\mathcal S_G\}\bigr)$.  Iterating the Lipschitz bounds for $\alpha$ and $\alpha^{-1}$ on word length gives $|\alpha^e(s)|_G\le D^{|e|}\le D^n$, so the element has $G$--length at most $nD^n$.  These estimates are first obtained at integer radii in the word metrics; the quasi-isometry constants from the Milnor--\v{S}varc lemma and the monotonicity of $\operatorname{Dist}(r)$ convert them, after changing the constants, into the stated inequalities for every real $r\ge1$.  See also \cite{NguyenSun} for distortion of subgroups of $3$--manifold groups.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:monodromy-energy}
For every $X\in\mathcal T$,
\[
h_{f^*X}=h_X\circ\phi,\qquad
\mathcal E(f^*X)=\mathcal E(X),\qquad
\Phi_{f^*X}=\phi^*\Phi_X.
\]
In particular $Z(\Phi)$ is invariant under the infinite cyclic group $\langle f\rangle$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The map $\phi:(S,\sigma_{f^*X})\to(S,\sigma_X)$ is an isometry, so $h_X\circ\phi$ is harmonic, and $h_X\circ\phi\simeq j\circ f\simeq j$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:markings}.  Theorem~\ref{thm:ESHartman} gives $h_{f^*X}=h_X\circ\phi$.  The other two identities follow because $\phi$ is an isometry and the Hopf differential is natural under pullback.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:GWproper}
The function $\mathcal E$ descends to a proper function
\(\overline{\mathcal E}:\mathcal T/\langle f\rangle\to\mathbb R\).
Equivalently, if $X_n\in\mathcal T$ and $\sup_n\mathcal E(X_n)<\infty$, then there are integers $k_n$ such that a subsequence of $(f^{k_n})^*X_n$ converges in $\mathcal T$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:energy-leastarea}
$\min_{X\in\mathcal T}\mathcal E(X)=A_0$.  Moreover $\mathcal E(X)=A_0$ if and only if $h_X$ is a least-area map homotopic to $j$; in that case $h_X$ is a conformal embedding onto a least-area fiber.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
For every smooth $u:(S,\sigma_X)\to M_f$ we have $E_X(u)\geq\operatorname{Area}(u)$, with equality if and only if $u$ is weakly conformal.  Hence
\(\mathcal E(X)=E_X(h_X)\geq\operatorname{Area}(h_X)\geq A_0\).
For a least-area fiber and $u_0$, $X_{\min}$ as in Section~4, Corollary~\ref{cor:Hopfzero} gives $h_{X_{\min}}=u_0$, so
\(\mathcal E(X_{\min})=E_{X_{\min}}(u_0)=\operatorname{Area}(u_0)=A_0\).
If $\mathcal E(X)=A_0$, both inequalities are equalities, so $h_X$ is weakly conformal and has least area in its homotopy class; by the discussion preceding Theorem~\ref{thm:leastarea} it is an embedding onto a least-area fiber.  The converse is the equality $\mathcal E(X_{\min})=A_0$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:minset}
The set of global minima of $\mathcal E$ is contained in $Z(\Phi)$.  It is the set of structures $(f^n)^*X_{\min}$, where $\Sigma_{\min}$ ranges over least-area fibers and $n\in\mathbb Z$, and its image in $\mathcal T/\langle f\rangle$ is compact.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The first two assertions follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:energy-leastarea}, Proposition~\ref{prop:monodromy-energy} and Lemma~\ref{lem:markings}.  The image is the closed subset $\overline{\mathcal E}^{-1}(A_0)$ of $\mathcal T/\langle f\rangle$, which is compact by Theorem~\ref{thm:GWproper}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:zero-orbit}
For a least-area fiber, the structures $(f^n)^*X_{\min}$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, are pairwise distinct points of $Z(\Phi)$, and they leave every compact subset of $\mathcal T$ as $|n|\to\infty$.  All of them correspond to the same surface $\Sigma_{\min}$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
A pseudo-Anosov mapping class has no fixed point in $\mathcal T$ and infinite order, and the mapping class group acts properly discontinuously on $\mathcal T$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:minimal-zero-injection}
Let $\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2\subset M_f$ be embedded minimal surfaces isotopic to the fiber, with conformal parametrizations $u_i:(S,X_i)\to\Sigma_i$ homotopic to $j$.  If $X_2=(f^n)^*X_1$ for some $n$, then $\Sigma_1=\Sigma_2$.  Thus $\Sigma\mapsto\langle f\rangle\cdot X_\Sigma$ is an injective map from embedded minimal surfaces isotopic to the fiber to $\langle f\rangle$--orbits in $Z(\Phi)$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The maps $u_i$ are conformal and minimal, hence harmonic, so $u_i=h_{X_i}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:ESHartman}.  By Proposition~\ref{prop:monodromy-energy}, $h_{X_2}=h_{X_1}\circ\phi^n$, so $\Sigma_2=u_2(S)=u_1(S)=\Sigma_1$.  The orbit $\langle f\rangle\cdot X_\Sigma$ does not depend on the choice of $u$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:markings}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:bounded-energy-escape}
Let $X_n\in\mathcal T$ with $\sup_n\mathcal E(X_n)<\infty$.  There are a compact set $K\subset\mathcal T$ and integers $k_n$ with $X_n\in(f^{-k_n})^*K$ for all $n$.  If $X_n$ leaves every compact subset of $\mathcal T$, then $|k_n|\to\infty$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The first statement is Theorem~\ref{thm:GWproper} together with the proper discontinuity of the action of $\langle f\rangle$.  If $|k_n|$ were bounded along a subsequence, that subsequence would lie in a finite union of translates of $K$, which is compact.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:Hopf-north-south}
Fix $X\in\mathcal T$ with $\Phi_X\neq0$, and let $[\mathcal F]\in\mathcal{PMF}(S)$ be the projective class of the vertical measured foliation of $\Phi_X$.  For $X_n=(f^n)^*X$, the vertical foliation of $\Phi_{X_n}=(\phi^n)^*\Phi_X$ has projective class $f^{-n}[\mathcal F]$.  Consequently, as $n\to+\infty$ these classes converge to $[\mathcal F^s]$ unless $[\mathcal F]=[\mathcal F^u]$, and as $n\to-\infty$ they converge to $[\mathcal F^u]$ unless $[\mathcal F]=[\mathcal F^s]$.  The same holds for horizontal foliations.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The identity for Hopf differentials is Proposition~\ref{prop:monodromy-energy}, and pullback of a quadratic differential by $\phi^n$ pulls back its vertical and horizontal measured foliations.  By the convention just fixed, this is the $f^{-n}$--orbit in $\mathcal{PMF}(S)$.  The asserted limits are therefore the north--south dynamics of the pseudo-Anosov class $f$: $[\mathcal F^u]$ is attracting and $[\mathcal F^s]$ is repelling for positive iterates of $f$ \cite{FLP}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:variational-CT}
Every $u\in\mathcal A_X$ extends continuously to $\mathbb H^2\cup S^1$ with boundary map $\partial\iota$.  The functional $E_X$ has a unique minimizer on $\mathcal A_X$, namely $\widetilde h_X$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The first statement is Proposition~\ref{prop:anyrepresentative}.  Elements of $\mathcal A_X$ are the lifts of the smooth maps $S\to M_f$ homotopic to $j$ (connect $u$ to $\widetilde j$ by the $\rho$--equivariant geodesic homotopy in $\mathbb H^3$), and $E_X(u)$ is the energy of the quotient map.  A harmonic map into a manifold of nonpositive curvature minimizes energy in its homotopy class, since energy is convex along geodesic homotopies; every minimizer is harmonic; and Theorem~\ref{thm:ESHartman} gives uniqueness.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:sameequiv}
The boundary maps of $\widetilde h_X$ for every $X\in\mathcal T$, and of the $\rho$--equivariant lift of every least-area fiber, induce the same equivalence relation $\sim_{CT}$ on $\partial G$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
Can the hyperbolic metric of $M_f$ together with the stable and unstable measured laminations be used to estimate $A_0$, or the distribution of $|A|^2$ on a least-area fiber, beyond the bounds $2\pi(g-1)<A_0<4\pi(g-1)$ and $\min|A|^2<2\le\max|A|^2$?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
Let $X_n\in\mathcal T$ with $\mathcal E(X_n)\to\infty$.  Which projective measured foliations occur as limits of the classes of the vertical foliations of $\Phi_{X_n}$?  Under what hypotheses are the only limits $[\mathcal F^s]$ and $[\mathcal F^u]$, and when do the rescaled equivariant maps $\widetilde h_{X_n}$ converge to an equivariant map to the dual $\mathbb R$--tree?
<!-- end question-2 -->
